Chapter 5: The Dangers of Dogmatism and the Value of Uncertainty.
Picture this. You’re in a busy office, and a team has gathered around a table to kick off a brand-new project. The manager stands firm, insisting there’s only one right way to move forward—shutting down any ideas that don’t fit the plan. Some people just nod along, not wanting to stir the pot, while others feel frustrated, watching good ideas get swept aside. The meeting wraps up, but instead of excitement, there’s this heavy feeling—like innovation just got boxed in by rigid thinking.
And honestly, dogmatism isn’t just something you find in the workplace. It creeps into science, religion, politics—even everyday conversations. Whenever we cling too tightly to our own beliefs, we risk shutting out fresh perspectives. Why does this happen? A lot of it comes from our natural craving for certainty. We all want clear answers, solid ground to stand on. But that quest for certainty can actually blind us, making us less open to new possibilities.
Most of the time, people don’t even realize when they’re slipping into dogmatic thinking. It might start with a little pride in being right, or maybe a fear of being wrong. Over time, those feelings turn into habits. Suddenly, questioning is discouraged, curiosity fades, and everyone just falls in line. The price? A culture where creativity dries up and the same mistakes keep happening, over and over.
There’s a story about a community facing a major crisis. The leaders clung to tradition, certain the old ways were best, and refused to try anything new. As things got worse, a few folks started to question whether sticking to the status quo really made sense. That created tension and division. But it wasn’t until a handful of brave voices spoke out—challenging what everyone “knew” to be true—that the community finally began to change.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: we often overlook the value of uncertainty. Most of us grow up being told to find answers, solve problems, and avoid doubt. But uncertainty isn’t the enemy—in fact, it’s a wellspring for creativity and growth. When we can admit we don’t have all the answers, suddenly we’re ready to learn. We start listening more closely, trying new things, and we’re less afraid to make mistakes.
In science, embracing uncertainty is absolutely essential. The biggest breakthroughs often come from daring to ask questions that don’t have easy answers. Researchers who challenge their own assumptions, test new ideas, and accept that failure is part of the process—they’re the ones who push things forward. And honestly, that’s true in every part of life, not just the lab.
The risks of dogmatism aren’t just intellectual—they’re emotional and social too. When being right matters more than anything, it can push people away, spark conflict, and close the door on building real connections. That hunger for certainty can actually block empathy and teamwork, making it harder to collaborate or understand where someone else is coming from.
Think about a parent who insists their way of raising kids is the only way. When their child starts to question those beliefs, the parent might feel threatened and react with anger. But after some reflection, that same parent might realize the power of listening—of being open to different perspectives and admitting they don’t have all the answers.
So, what’s the real value of uncertainty? It keeps us humble. It reminds us that no one knows everything, that learning never really ends, and that every answer is just a stepping stone. By embracing uncertainty, we open ourselves up to resilience, creativity, and compassion. And in a world that’s always changing, isn’t that exactly what we need?
